name: Ishiwari-zakura (The Rock-Splitting Cherry)
species: Edo Higan Cherry (Prunus itosakura, syn. Cerasus spachiana)

location.address: Uchimaru 9-1, grounds of Morioka District Court, Morioka, Iwate Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, on the public grounds of the Morioka District Court in front of the courthouse building; open to visitors daily, dogs must stay outside the grounds. No ticket, appointment or reception needed.
transport: About 15-20 minutes on foot from JR Morioka Station
verify_notes: One of Japan's most famous individual cherry trees, a genuine standalone destination (highest demand of this batch, 523 reads/month across 2 language Wikipedias; covered by Japan National Tourism Organization's own travel site, Atlas Obscura, Voyapon etc). Grows from a crack in a large granite boulder in the front garden of the Morioka District Court; legend says the boulder was split by lightning and cherry seeds caught in the crack. Designated a national Natural Monument on 7 March 1923 (Taisho 12). 1995 official measurement: root/base circumference (measured within the rock split, not a standard trunk girth) 4.3 m, height 10.8 m, canopy spread 8.8m E / 8.4m W / 5.5m S / 7.3m N -> girth_cm recorded as 430 with that caveat. Age: city and Wikipedia sources both describe it as roughly 350 to 400+ years old across different years of reporting rather than a single fixed figure (age at last formal measurement, 1995, was given as approximately 350 years; adding years since, plus the wider 350-400 year range still used in the city's own current visitor notice, gives the broad estimate used here). Species is Edo Higan (Prunus itosakura / Cerasus spachiana / older name Prunus subhirtella var. subhirtella; taxonomy has shifted names over the decades, all refer to the same tree). Survived a 1932 fire that burned part of the courthouse; gardener Fujimura Jitaro protected the trunk with a wet coat and it bloomed again the following spring, which is the anecdote worth leading with alongside the boulder-splitting story. A special bus parking area opens for the blossom season (5-11 April window, weather dependent). Coordinates cross-checked: Wikipedia gives 39 42 13.7 N 141 9 4.2 E, which converts to 39.70380, 141.15117, matching the given pin to within a few metres, both landing inside the district court grounds where the tree visibly stands, confirmed at tree level. Flagged only because the exact current-year age is an estimate drawn from source years that do not perfectly agree, not because of any doubt about identity, species or whether it is alive (routinely photographed and reported on every blossom season, most recently in April 2026 news coverage).

name: Ishito no Kaba-zakura
species: Kaba-zakura, a natural hybrid of Edo Higan and Yamazakura cherries (Cerasus x kabazakura, syn. Cerasus subhirtella x Cerasus serrulata)

location.address: Ishito-shuku 3-119, grounds of Tokoji Temple, Kitamoto, Saitama Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, on the grounds of Tokoji Temple; the city runs an on-site cherry-blossom festival with 120 parking spaces during the bloom window. No ticket or appointment needed.
transport: Bus or taxi from JR Kita-Kounosu or Kitamoto Station; no direct rail access to Ishito-shuku
verify_notes: A genuine standalone destination on its own merits: one of Japan's 'Five Great Cherry Trees' (Nihon Go-dai Zakura), and the only known specimen anywhere of this natural Edo Higan x Yamazakura hybrid, called Kaba-zakura after Minamoto no Noriyori (nicknamed 'Kaba no Kanja'), who legend says planted the seed here in the late 12th century. Designated a national Natural Monument on 12 October 1922; Tokoji temple grounds, Kitamoto, Saitama. Girth/height figures differ slightly by source and year: a 2023 Saitama Shimbun news article (marking the tree's 100th year as a designated monument) gives trunk circumference approx. 7 m and height approx. 12 m; Japanese Wikipedia gives root circumference approx. 7.2 m and height approx. 12 m. girth_cm recorded as 710 (midpoint of the 700-720cm range both sources agree on). Age is the long-repeated 'approximately 800 years' figure used by both the city and Wikipedia; treated here as a vague-but-real estimate rather than sharpened further, per the age rules. History of decline and active conservation is worth keeping for the story: the tree had four trunks until the 1960s-70s, was reduced to one by soil compaction and stress from ten stone memorial tablets (itazutoba) placed at its roots, which were removed in 1973; it did not flower for ten years and bloomed again in 1977 after the removal; the city has been improving the soil with liquid fertiliser injections since 2004 and expanded the protected ground in 2022 by acquiring an adjacent private plot for the root system. Confirmed alive and cared for as of the 2023 news article (crowds at full bloom) and the city's own current visitor page (free admission, parking for the blossom season, updated periodically); the '1923' in one candidate photo filename is the photograph's own capture year (public domain, pre-1956), not evidence about today, and was NOT used as alive-today evidence. Coordinates: a geotagged 2013 Commons/Panoramio photo of the tree itself carries 36.006663, 139.512355, within a few metres of the given pin, and a Nominatim reverse lookup of the given coordinate lands on a residential road in Ishito-shuku 3-chome matching the official address; both the geotagged photo of the actual tree and the address match support tree-level (confirmed) precision even though no OSM node exists for this small temple site.

name: Yuya no Naga Fuji (the Long Wisteria of Yuya)

location.address: 330 Ikeda, grounds of Gyokoji Temple, Iwata, Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, on the grounds of Gyokoji Temple, Ikeda, Iwata. The city runs a wisteria festival with temporary riverside parking during the mid-to-late April bloom window; the temple garden is otherwise open to visitors.
transport: Bus or taxi from JR Iwata or Fukude station; no direct rail access to Ikeda
verify_notes: IMPORTANT NAMING NOTE FOR THE WRITER: the tree's kanji name is 熊野の長フジ/熊野の長藤. The kanji 熊野 is usually read 'Kumano' but is read locally as 'Yuya' here (confirmed by multiple Japanese sources giving the reading as yuya no nagafuji), after Yuya Gozen (also called Kumano Gozen), a late-Heian-period court woman from Ikeda who, by temple legend, planted the wisteria herself before going on to serve Taira no Munemori in Kyoto; the Noh play 'Yuya' is about her, and an OSM information board at the site is titled 'the Noh play Yuya and Gyokoji Temple', which is corroborating evidence for the local reading. Do not silently 'correct' the name to Kumano. A standalone destination: this is one of Japan's most celebrated wisterias, subject of an annual dedicated festival (Ikeda's Yuya-no-Nagafuji Matsuri) with night illumination, extensive tourism-board and newspaper coverage every spring including 2025/2026 event listings, which is strong evidence it is alive and actively maintained now. Designated a national Natural Monument on 25 July 1932 (one specimen); five further wisteria plants on the same temple grounds hold a separate prefectural designation from 26 September 1972 (each roughly 250 years old, not part of this entry). Officially managed by Iwata City since 7 March 1967. Girth conflict between sources: the official Agency for Cultural Affairs heritage database (online.bunka.go.jp) and Japanese Wikipedia both give root circumference as approximately 1.8 m (180cm), which is what girth_cm records; a third source (a private Shizuoka sightseeing blog) gave 2.9 m (290cm) for what it called 'root circumference', which does not match either primary/official source and is not used, flagging this tree per the sources-conflict rule. Flower clusters on this specimen reach over 1 m long, with a recorded maximum of 1.5 m and historic reports of up to 2 m, and the trellis area has grown from roughly 400 sqm in 1907 to about 1,600 sqm today including the adjoining Toyoda Yuya Memorial Park. Age given consistently as approximately 800-850 years since the Heian-period planting legend; treated as a vague source-given estimate rather than sharpened. Coordinates: the given pin sits about 35m from an OSM information board specifically about Yuya Gozen and Gyokoji Temple, and about 70m from the temple building itself (OSM way, amenity=place_of_worship, name Gyokoji-ji); a Nominatim reverse lookup lands correctly in Ikeda, Iwata. This is close enough, on a small single-site temple garden whose whole point is this wisteria trellis, to mark confirmed rather than approximate, though there is no coordinate pinned to the vine's own base specifically.
